title: Model evidence rubric and sales anchors
content:
Purpose and audience:

- Quick working brief for GTM, sales enablement, and product marketing to articulate why Redwood’s model catalog (with verified profiles) is differentiated for engineering-led buyers evaluating open models.
- Audience: product-led growth users evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, platform/infra buyers, and technical buyers (ML Engineers, Platform Engineers).

Executive snapshot (one-paragraph):
Redwood’s model catalog is not just a directory — it’s an evidence-driven decision surface. For teams choosing open models, the biggest seller is predictable economics and risk reduction: verified performance profiles (latency, cost, quality on benchmarked tasks), deployment compatibility (quantization/FP16 footprints), and operational playbooks (fallbacks, cache configs). Positioning should emphasize: measurable trade-offs, real-world benchmarks, and prescriptive selection guidance that maps to customers’ product constraints (latency SLOs, cost per 1M tokens, and quality thresholds).

Core narrative pillars (how to talk about it):
- Predictable outcomes: show customers a small set of metrics that actually map to their decision (p50/p95 latency, throughput on x GPUs, tokens/sec, cost-per-token at X batch size).
- Evidence-first verification: verified profiles are not trust badges — they’re replicable test harnesses + runbooks we share under NDA/free trial to reproduce results on their workloads.
- Operational alignment: pick a model not just for quality, but for how it fits into their serving constraints (KV cache behavior, quantization compatibility, memory + temperature sensitivity).
- Safety and degradation paths: highlight fallback rules, variant pairing (lower-cost quantized variant), and regional routing to maintain SLAs.

Competitive analysis notes (quick hits):
- Major cloud providers: often show raw throughput but opaque tuning details. Weakness: customer doesn’t get a reproducible performance story for their prompt distributions.
- Pure-play LLM APIs: sell simplicity. Weakness: limited transparency on underlying model variants and fewer tools to tune for cost/latency.
- Open-source runtimes / OSS inference: powerful but high ops burden; weakness is tooling integration for ramping to production (rollouts, tracing, per-route cost).

Where Redwood wins:
- Unified serving + observability: same APIs across hosted/dedicated/private; evidence can be run across these modes so customers can trust handoffs.
- Prescriptive model pairing: we recommend exact quantization profiles + batch configs for each verified profile.
- Focus on metrics buyers care about: show delta in cost/latency for a single change (e.g., switch to 4-bit quantized variant -> 40% cost reduction with <3% ROUGE drop on X).

Model evidence rubric (working draft — use to score and prioritize catalog entries)
- Purpose: create a short, repeatable rubric that sales/solutions can reference when advising customers. Score each model 0–5 on each dimension; compute weighted total.

Rubric dimensions and suggested weights (sum = 100):
- Latency predictability (20): reproducible p50/p95 given typical prompt lengths.
- Cost-efficiency (15): tokens/sec per GPU, cost per 1M tokens with recommended config.
- Quality on vertical tasks (20): measured by task-suite (instructions, summarization, extraction) relevant to buyer.
- Stability / determinism (10): variance across seeds/temperature and behavior with long context.
- Quantization friendliness (10): measured recompression loss and ops compatibility (4-bit, 8-bit).
- Footprint & deployment fit (10): memory, shardability, hardware affinity (A100 vs H100 vs commodity).
- Safety & hallucination profile (10): empirical hallucination rate on extraction tasks and known failure modes.
- Documentation / reproducibility (5): presence of reproducible harness and example configs.

Scoring example (fictional):
Model: OpenLM-XL-Turbo-v1
- Latency predictability: 4
- Cost-efficiency: 3
- Quality vertical: 4
- Stability: 3
- Quant-friendliness: 5
- Footprint: 4
- Safety: 2
- Documentation: 5
Weighted total = 3.7/5 (normalized).

Why a compact rubric matters:
- Sales needs a clear one-page answer: "if you need sub-200ms p95 at 256 tokens, we recommend X with config Y".
- The rubric supports automation: scoring feeds model-catalog filters and search facets for customers.

Sales anchor language (short snippets for 30–90s buyer conversations)
- For engineering leads focused on latency: "We surface models with verified p95 numbers measured on our serving runtime so you can compare apples-to-apples. If you need sub-200ms p95 at 256 tokens, here are three models we’ve validated in both hosted and private modes — plus exact configs to reproduce the numbers."
- For infra/platform teams concerned about cost: "We recommend a quantized companion for every high-quality model — customers routinely drop per-token cost by ~30–50% with minimal quality regressions, and we include the rollout safety playbook."
- For product PMs worried about hallucinations: "Our verified profiles include targeted extraction and hallucination tests. We’ll show you failure cases and give you remediation patterns (prompt engineering + reranking + guardrail models)."

Objection handling cheatsheet (common objections + concise responses)
- Objection: "Open models are risky / variable."  Response: "We don’t treat them as black boxes — our verified profiles are the test harness + recommended runtime settings so customers can reproduce the same results in their environment."
- Objection: "We need enterprise support / SLAs."  Response: "Dedicated and Private modes come with SLA options and escalation playbooks; models are paired to guaranteed throughput profiles in Dedicated pools."
- Objection: "How do we choose among dozens of open models?" Response: "We map your constraints (latency, cost, vertical tasks) to a short list using the rubric and run a two-week trial with sample prompts to collect real delta metrics."

Go-to-market experiments to validate messaging (priority order)
1) Sales play A/B: give two SDR scripts (evidence-first vs benefit-first) and measure conversion on proof-of-concept requests over 6 weeks.
2) Website microcopy: add a "verified performance" filter with short artifacts — track clicks-to-trial.
3) Whitepaper + reproducible kit: offer a downloadable demo harness for three models; gate detailed configs behind lead capture.
4) Field packet for SEs: 2-page cheat for one vertical (search assistants) with 3 recommended models and rollout commands — measure time-to-proof and deal cycle.

Operational next steps (owner: Maya Chen)
- Finalize rubric weights with product and serving runtime (target: 2-week sync).
- Create template reproducible harness (Docker + sample prompts + perf script) for every new catalog entry.
- Build two-page SE battle-card derived from the above sales anchors (owner: Ethan Park).
- Ship a microsite filter for "verified p95" and track CTRs (owner: Sofia Alvarez).

Open questions / risks (notes for product):
- How much of the reproducible harness can be public vs NDA gated? Need legal input.
- Resource cost of running heavy benchmarks for every model and variant; consider priority tiers.
- Balancing transparency with IP concerns and partner model licensing terms.

Appendix: quick checklist for adding a verified profile (working)
- Basic metadata + model artifact link (repo/model card)
- Run standard perf harness (3 prompt distributions: short, medium, long) — capture p50/p95, tokens/sec.
- Run vertical task-suite (instructions, summarization, extraction) and record quality metrics and failure examples.
- Run quantization experiments and record delta in cost/quality.
- Produce a 1-page profile (metrics + recommended runtime config + rollout notes).
- Assign rubric score and publish to catalog as "verified (internal)" or "verified (public)".

Notes to self: keep this doc alive as we iterate on the rubric. The goal is not to have every model scored on day 1, but to make the choice process repeatable and defensible for prospects.

-- end --
